strengths: Valuable benchmark contribution of the Datasets/Benchmarks type: unifying eight public staged fall datasets (~14 h, 101 subjects, 29 views) under a consistent ten-class taxonomy that separates transient actions from static states addresses a genuine and long-standing fragmentation problem in fall detection research, where incompatible annotation schemes have prevented fair cross-dataset comparison.

The systematic, PRISMA-guided dataset search and the explicit documentation of excluded datasets (with reasons: licenses, viewpoint incompatibility, static images) adds transparency and improves reproducibility of the curation process.

The staged-to-wild protocol using OOPS-Fall, curated from genuine accident videos in the OOPS dataset, is a thoughtful and novel evaluation design; the paper convincingly demonstrates meaningful in-distribution vs. in-the-wild performance gaps that existing single-dataset evaluations could not reveal.

The experimental analysis is reasonably thorough: cross-subject and cross-view splits, domain-shift analysis via pairwise FVD and embedding visualizations, three frozen backbones, multi-granular evaluation tasks (10-class, fall, fallen, fall∪fallen), and a temporal action segmentation baseline (MS-TCN++). The finding that I3D generalizes best OOD despite weaker in-distribution accuracy is an interesting and actionable insight.
The paper includes a meaningful limitations section (demographic bias, limited wild scenarios, privacy) and a genuine societal-impact discussion, appropriate for an elder-care application.
weaknesses: Annotation quality assurance is under-specified. The claim of 're-annotating all staged datasets' under a new taxonomy is the core contribution, yet the paper reports no details on the annotation process: number of annotators, annotation guidelines, inter-annotator agreement, or verification procedure for the re-labeling of thousands of segments. For a benchmark paper, this is a substantive evidentiary gap.

The OOPS-Fall binary fall/no-fall labels may not be semantically equivalent to the staged taxonomy (e.g., distinguishing 'fall' from 'lie down', or 'fallen' states). The paper does not discuss this label-definition mismatch between the staged source domain and the wild test set, which could confound the interpretation of the staged-to-wild gap as a pure domain shift.

Baselines are limited to frozen backbones with a lightweight temporal transformer head. No fine-tuned baselines, no state-of-the-art action recognition models (e.g., larger VideoMAE variants, InternVideo), and no comparison with published fall detection methods. While frozen-feature analysis is a defensible design choice for benchmarking representations, it limits conclusions about attainable performance on OmniFall and the practical relevance of the reported gap magnitudes.

Reproducibility information is incomplete in the submission: the code and dataset links in the abstract are placeholders, and details such as how OOPS-Fall segments were filtered/verified (1.3k from 20k videos) and how 'other' class boundaries were decided are only sketched. Whether OmniFall can be legally redistributed (vs. download scripts) is not discussed.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: inconsistent bold marking across Tables 2-3, OCCU cross-view 'Fallen' F1 of 0.00 discussed only in passing, MCFD's role in cross-subject evaluation (single subject, training only) makes its inclusion in per-dataset results confusing, and 'excempt'/'a overfitting' typos indicate insufficient proofreading.

The segmentation evaluation uses only one method (MS-TCN++ with I3D) on only the cross-subject split, so the temporal segmentation track of the benchmark is under-validated relative to the classification track.

strengths: Genuinely useful aggregation effort: unifying eight public staged fall datasets (~14h unique footage, 101 subjects, 29 views) under one ten-class taxonomy addresses a real fragmentation problem in the field, and the systematic PRISMA-based search is a commendable, more rigorous approach to dataset selection than is typical.

The staged-to-wild evaluation protocol using OOPS-Fall (genuine accidents curated from OOPS) is a valuable and novel contribution; the resulting finding that frozen I3D generalizes to in-the-wild falls while stronger in-distribution VideoMAE models collapse (Se 0.68 vs 0.15-0.21) is an interesting and actionable insight.

Well-motivated taxonomy design that separates transient actions from persistent static states, directly targeting the medically relevant 'long-lie' fallen-state detection rather than only fall events.

Standardized cross-subject and cross-view splits with per-dataset protocols are documented in reasonable detail, and domain-shift analysis (FVD, t-SNE/H-NNE) supports the qualitative claims about dataset clustering.
Honest limitations and societal-impact discussions are present, correctly identifying demographic bias, privacy, and surveillance concerns.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is undermined in a benchmark paper where it matters most: the abstract's 'OmniFall:' and 'Code:' entries are empty placeholders with no URL, and no annotation guidelines, inter-annotator agreement statistics, or quality-control protocol for the re-annotation of eight datasets are reported. For a dataset contribution, this is a substantive shortcoming, not a cosmetic one.

The baseline evaluation is too narrow to support the claim of a 'comprehensive evaluation of generalization capabilities'. Only frozen backbones with a lightweight classification head are tested; no fine-tuned models, no domain adaptation/alignment methods, and no pose/skeleton-based approaches (the de facto standard in fall detection) are included, so the benchmark's value for future comparisons is not demonstrated.

The paper is the main bottleneck: Tables 2-3 are dense and difficult to parse, Table 4 is never shown in the provided pages (only referenced), the symbol 'Δ' in table headers is undefined, and Table 2 contains outright internal inconsistencies (e.g., CMDFall CS Fall F1 0.88 exceeds what Sensitivity/Specificity of 0.84/0.99 would typically support; Oops-Fall CS specificity is blank but CV shows 0.63 alongside 0.82 Se while the text claims specificity >0.98 across all domains). Such inconsistencies, if real, erode confidence in the experimental pipeline.

OOPS-Fall is only binary (fall/no fall) and does not use the paper's own ten-class taxonomy, creating a label-space mismatch between the staged superset and the wild test set; the curation of 1.3k segments from OOPS is also not described in enough detail (annotator count, agreement, filtering criteria beyond 'original tags').

Several factual inconsistencies between text and Table 1 (e.g., Le2i resolution stated as 640x480 in Section 2 but 320x240 in Table 1; '143 staged falls' vs 222 recordings) and minor description errors (MCFD '22 fall scenarios' vs 24 recordings) suggest insufficient proofreading for a dataset paper whose tables are its core product.

Missing fairness/ethics treatment of redistribution rights: many aggregated datasets have restrictive or ambiguous licenses (the authors themselves note they had to exclude four datasets for this reason), yet no discussion of the licensing status of the eight included datasets or of consent/privacy for identifiable subjects in the staged footage and OOPS videos is provided.

Experimental asymmetries (CaucaFall appears only in CS rows, MCFD only in CV rows in Tables 2-3, OCCU CV Fallen Se = 0.00 for I3D) are not explained, and the 'Overall' rows mix datasets with very different sizes, so aggregate numbers are hard to interpret.

The claim that I3D's simplicity 'explains' its OOD superiority is speculative; with only three backbones and frozen features, alternative explanations (resolution, frame rate, pre-training data overlap) are not controlled for.

strengths: As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the core resource is genuinely valuable: unifying eight public fall detection datasets (~14h of recordings, 101 subjects, 29 camera views) under a consistent ten-class taxonomy that separates transient actions from persistent states addresses a real and well-motivated gap, since incompatible annotation schemes have prevented fair cross-dataset comparison in this field.

The dataset search is conducted systematically following PRISMA guidelines, with clear inclusion/exclusion criteria and transparent documentation of why other datasets (UR Fall, MUVIM, FPDS, High Quality FSD, FallFree, SIMPLE, ACT42) were excluded — this is above-average rigor for benchmark papers.

The OOPS-Fall curation from genuine accident videos and the staged-to-wild protocol is the most original element: it provides the first in-the-wild test set for fall detection and quantifies a concrete deployment-relevant domain gap that staged benchmarks cannot capture.

The evaluation is reasonably comprehensive for a benchmark paper: three frozen backbones, cross-subject and cross-view splits, multiple granularities (10-class, binary fall, fallen, union), plus temporal segmentation with MS-TCN++, with detailed metric tables enabling future comparison.

The finding that frozen I3D generalizes best OOD while VideoMAE variants overfit to the staged distribution is an interesting, actionable insight for the community, supported by FVD analysis and embedding visualizations.
The paper includes a meaningful limitations section and a thoughtful societal impact discussion (surveillance, false alarms, demographic disparities).
weaknesses: Reproducibility is currently not established: the 'OmniFall:' and 'Code:' links in the abstract are empty, and no release page is given. For a benchmark paper whose entire value lies in community access to the annotations and splits, this is a serious gap at submission time.

The baseline analysis is limited to frozen backbones with a lightweight classification head. No fine-tuned models, no modern video LLMs, and no comparison against published fall-detection methods are included, so the community cannot judge whether the reported gaps reflect representation quality or benchmark difficulty. The claimed OOD insight about I3D rests on only three backbones and deserves deeper analysis.

Annotation quality is under-reported: the paper re-annotates all eight datasets into a new taxonomy but gives no details on annotator protocol, inter-annotator agreement, or validation of label consistency across datasets with very different original schemas. For a benchmark contribution, this is a key evidence gap.

The stated motivation of enabling 'fair cross-dataset comparison' is only partially delivered: the main experiments train on the union of all staged datasets rather than the informative train-on-X/test-on-Y cross-dataset matrix that the unified taxonomy would uniquely permit.

OOPS-Fall is binary-only (fall/no fall), which limits comparability with the ten-class taxonomy and leaves ambiguity about whether 'fallen state' is detectable on wild data — arguably the medically most critical class per the paper's own motivation. The curation procedure (1.3k segments from 20k videos) also lacks detail on filtering bias and negative-segment selection.

Some results raise questions that are not discussed: GMDCSA24 near-chance 10-class performance for all backbones, OCCU cross-view 'Fallen' Se=0.00 for I3D, and the unclear OOPS-Fall rows (metric headers absent in Tables 2–3, no specificity for OOPS-Fall). These need explanation or correction.

Presentation has notable sloppiness: typos ('excempt', 'a overfitting', 'accross'), empty link placeholders, incomplete reference fields (missing venues/years for [1], [3], [10], [14], [15], [17]), and dense radar plots (Figure 6) that are hard to read.

The staged-to-wild domain gap confounds multiple factors (camera quality, demographics, falls-with-props vs. genuine accidents); the paper acknowledges this qualitatively but provides no controlled disentanglement, weakening causal interpretation of the OOD numbers.

strengths: Substantial curation and annotation effort: unifying eight public staged datasets under a single 16-class frame-level taxonomy (14 h staged, 818 verified in-the-wild videos, 12k synthetic videos) with dense per-frame labels, standardized cross-subject/cross-view splits, and documented multi-view annotation transfer is a genuine service to the fall-detection community, which has long suffered from incompatible label sets and protocols.

The benchmark design is well-motivated: the staged → wild gap is isolated via a test-only in-the-wild set (OF-ItW), enabling OOD evaluation that prior fall datasets cannot support; the taxonomy's explicit distinction of transient 'fall' vs. persistent 'fallen' states is clinically meaningful.

The experimental section goes beyond simple dataset release: domain-shift analysis (FVD across three backbones, t-SNE/H-NNE visualizations), controlled cross-domain fine-tuning experiments (CMDFall vs. OF-Staged vs. OF-Syn vs. combined), and timeline-segmentation (ASQuery) with motion- vs. appearance-centric features yield a nuanced finding (synthetic appearance diversity helps frame-space features; staged dynamics help motion-space features) rather than a single over-simplified claim.

Thorough reproducibility scaffolding: PRISMA-guided dataset search, explicit licensing/permission documentation for all sources, deterministic synthetic attribute assignment, detailed split definitions, feature-extraction configurations, and quality-assurance protocol for the ~33 h of annotations.
Appropriate contribution type (Datasets/Benchmarks) with meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussions, including the gender/age bias concerns of synthetic data and deployment ethics.

The cross-attribute splits (cross-age, cross-ethnicity, cross-BMI) on OF-Syn are a useful bonus for probing demographic robustness in a domain where real data on vulnerable populations is ethically hard to collect.
weaknesses: The headline claim that 'synthetic data can match or surpass real staged footage on cross-domain transfer' rests on a single architecture (VideoMAE-K400) and one segmentation model (ASQuery); no comparison against established fall-detection methods or even a second video model for classification, so generality of the synthetic-vs-staged conclusion is not established.

The FVD/t-SNE evidence that OF-Syn is closest to OF-ItW in feature space, combined with OF-Syn's better OF-ItW performance, raises a possible confound: similarity in appearance statistics to the specific OOPS-derived test set may partly drive the result rather than genuine fall-relevant generalization. The paper notes the correlation but does not disentangle it (e.g., by testing on a second wild source or by controlling for appearance statistics).

OF-ItW is test-only and derived from OOPS, whose clips capture many kinds of unintentional actions in uncontrolled settings; the curation/verification criteria for what counts as a genuine fall (and label reliability on this noisy source) are only briefly described ('manually verify'), and inter-annotator agreement statistics are not reported for any subset.

Multi-view annotations were produced on one primary view and transferred to synchronized views without per-view verification; the paper does not quantify the annotation error this may introduce, particularly for occluded views in OCCU-like scenarios.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness reduce clarity: the abstract claims '80 hours / 15k videos' while the body/appendix report ~33 h single-view (82 h multi-view) and different video counts; the cross-ethnicity split's arbitrary mapping of training vs. test groups is statistically fragile (and the group definitions mix race and region); minor text artifacts in figures (e.g., Figure 6 caption text) suggest insufficient proofreading.

Class-imbalance handling and metric choices are somewhat ad hoc: per-class 'Fall/Fallen' binary subtasks are thresholded and reported per dataset, but macro-F1 across 16 classes is dominated by rare classes; the paper would benefit from per-class confidence intervals or seeds/averaging to support conclusions like the +1.4 F1 gain from combined training, which is within noise range.

Release is promised 'upon acceptance' — a weaker reproducibility guarantee than an anonymized release; given that the benchmark's value is contingent on public availability of the harmonized annotations (not the underlying videos, which are licensed), the labels/splits/code should be verifiable at review time.

The synthetic component's generative provenance (Wan 2.2) embeds the biases of that model (acknowledged for expressions), but there is no quantitative audit of how faithfully the generated actions match the intended taxonomy (e.g., fraction of 'fall' videos where a fall actually occurs), which matters because the dataset is proposed as a training source.

strengths: Genuinely useful unification effort: re-annotating eight heterogeneous public fall-detection datasets into a harmonized 16-class, frame-level taxonomy with cross-subject and cross-view splits addresses a real, well-documented reproducibility problem in this field.

The benchmark design is thoughtful: a test-only in-the-wild split (OF-ItW) enables staged→wild and synthetic→wild OOD evaluation that prior fragmented datasets could not support, and supporting both classification and timeline segmentation broadens applicability.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive for a benchmark paper: multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-K400, SigLIP2), FVD-based domain-shift analysis, ablations over training sources (staged, synthetic, combined), and demographic cross-splits (age, BMI, ethnicity) on the synthetic data.

The headline finding — synthetic data closing the staged→wild gap better than staged data, with appearance- vs motion-centric feature complementarity — is interesting and could influence how scarce, ethically sensitive elder-care data is collected.

Exemplary diligence on licensing/permissions for all eight source datasets, a PRISMA-documented search process, honest limitations section, and a societal-impact discussion covering surveillance, false alarms, and demographic bias.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited: two of the three components are aggregations or re-annotations of already-public data (eight staged sets; OF-ItW is filtered/re-annotated OOPS). The genuinely new asset is the Wan 2.2-generated synthetic set, whose realism and long-term value as a benchmark resource is unproven.

The in-the-wild test set is small (2.6 h, 818 videos, ~10–20 videos per class in samples) and its composition is not characterized in detail (subject demographics, scene types, fall frequency), which weakens the central staged→wild generalization claims drawn from it.

Baseline coverage is narrow: essentially one fine-tuned model (VideoMAE-K400) plus one segmentation method (ASQuery) and frozen-feature analyses. Claims that the benchmark 'exposes challenging staged→wild transfer' would be far more convincing with a broader set of modern video models or at least pose/skeleton-based fall detectors, which are standard in this literature.

Some headline results are less strong than the abstract suggests: the best combined training yields only +1.4 F1 over synthetic alone on the wild set, and absolute wild-set performance remains low (Fall F1 ~60–66%), leaving open whether the benchmark is well-posed or simply too hard given the test set's size.

Presentation inconsistencies undermine confidence: the abstract claims 80 hours/15k videos while the body reports 33 h single-view (82 h multi-view) and 12k synthetic videos; the 'Fallen' category and 16-class taxonomy boundaries (e.g., lie_down vs fallen) are asserted as a key contribution but inter-annotator agreement or label-quality statistics are not quantified.
Code and data are only promised 'upon acceptance'; without an anonymized release at review time, reproducibility of the annotation pipeline and splits cannot be verified.

Synthetic-data ethics framing is somewhat overstated: generation relies on demographic stereotypes (age-to-environment/clothing mappings) that may introduce new biases, and the paper's own cross-age results show marked sensitivity drops for toddlers and the elderly — the population that matters most.

strengths: Substantial and well-motivated benchmark contribution: unifying eight public staged datasets under a harmonized 16-class per-frame taxonomy, adding a 12k-video synthetic set with controlled demographic diversity, and providing the first test-only in-the-wild fall benchmark is a genuine service to the fall-detection community, which has long suffered from incompatible annotations and protocols.

Careful and transparent curation methodology: a PRISMA-guided systematic search, explicit documentation of licensing/permissions for every source dataset (appendix A.1), dataset-specific cross-subject and cross-view splits that mirror original protocols, and a combined split enable principled cross-domain comparison.

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: the paper goes beyond releasing data, providing domain-shift analysis (FVD matrices on three backbone feature types, t-SNE/H-NNE visualizations), supervised fall/action classification (four training configurations), and timeline segmentation (ASQuery with two frozen feature families, plus unsupervised baselines). The experiments directly test the benchmark's core claims.

Interesting and useful empirical findings: the result that synthetic data transfers better to in-the-wild footage than staged data (Fall F1 60.5–61.2% vs. 52.3%), that diversity rather than volume drives generalization, and the complementary roles of appearance-centric vs. motion-centric features for the synthetic→real shift are actionable insights for practitioners.

Good completeness of the dataset documentation: detailed split definitions, annotation workflow (VIA-based, multi-view transfer strategy, two-pass QA), synthetic generation pipeline with deterministic attribute seeding, and feature-extraction configurations support reproducibility.
Honest limitations section and a thoughtful societal-impact discussion covering surveillance concerns, false-alarm trust erosion, and demographic bias—appropriate for a safety-relevant application.
weaknesses: Inconsistent headline statistics undermine confidence in bookkeeping: the abstract claims 80 hours / 15k videos and 60h staged, the intro says ~33h single-view / 14h staged recordings, and Fig. 1 shows 60/17/2.6h. These may be reconcilable (multi-view vs. single-view accounting), but the paper never clearly reconciles them; a single consistent accounting table is needed.

No quantitative annotation-quality metrics are reported. The multi-view label-transfer strategy (annotating one primary view and propagating to synchronized cameras) is efficient but error-prone; no inter-annotator agreement, boundary tolerance statistics, or audit numbers are given, despite frame-level labels being the benchmark's core value.

The claim that 'synthetic can match or surpass staged data' needs more nuance: both OF-Syn and OF-ItW are web/diffusion-derived visual distributions, so the smaller synthetic→wild gap may partly reflect shared appearance statistics of web-sourced OOPS footage rather than genuine demographic bridging. A confound analysis or an additional wild source would strengthen the headline claim.

Synthetic attribute labels are prompt-specified but never visually verified (age, ethnicity, BMI are generation parameters, not annotated appearance), so cross-age/cross-BMI split results (Fig. 7) may be affected by label noise; this caveat should be made explicit.

Baseline coverage is narrow: end-to-end fine-tuning uses only VideoMAE-K400, and segmentation uses only ASQuery. More method diversity (e.g., pose-based fall detectors, which are common in this field, or a second video model) would make the benchmark conclusions more robust.

Reproducibility is promised 'upon acceptance' rather than released with the submission; no validation that splits and annotations actually run end-to-end. Error bars/statistical significance are absent for all comparisons, some of which involve margins of only 1–2 F1 points.

Minor presentation issues: several typos and incomplete sentences (e.g., the 'OOPS!' dataset description is cut off mid-sentence, Fig. 6 caption has a broken sentence), and Table 2's OF-ItW rows evaluated with CS training only make some cross-table comparisons confusing.
